canonical_topic: Mode, median, and mean as measures of central tendency
definition: Mode, median, and mean are the three standard ways to describe the 'typical' value of a distribution: the most frequent value, the midpoint value, and the arithmetic average, respectively.
core_idea: Each measure has a different practical tradeoff: mode is the most frequent value but can be ambiguous (multiple modes) and expensive to find; median is the true midpoint but requires sorting the full data set; mean is the simple average and is the easiest and cheapest to compute, which is why it is treated as the most important of the three.
key_points: Mode = value(s) occurring most often; a distribution can have more than one mode (e.g., a fair coin flip has heads and tails as co-equal modes).
Mode is rarely used in practice because finding it requires scanning the whole distribution and it isn't guaranteed to be unique.
Median = the value splitting the distribution into top 50% and bottom 50%; for an even number of samples it is the average of the two middle values.
Median's practical drawback is that computing it requires sorting the data set, which is slow for very large sets even on fast computers.
Mean (arithmetic mean) = sum of all values divided by count; it represents the expected value of a random variable.
Mean's main advantage is ease of calculation, which is why the author calls it the most important central-tendency measure.
Mode, median, and mean do not necessarily coincide — different distribution shapes can pull them apart, though the mode always sits at a distribution's peak(s).
relationships: Mean is the reference point used later in the mean absolute deviation and variance formulas.
trading_implications: Mean is favored in practice for describing 'typical' price behavior (e.g., typical neighborhood gasoline price) because it is cheap and simple to compute at scale.
caveats: Assuming mode, median, and mean will agree for a given distribution — they can diverge depending on the distribution's shape.
